# Introduction to the model

The Log-Normal Race model [LNR; @rouderLognormalRaceCognitiveProcess2015] is
a race model for choice response time data. Each response option has its own
accumulator, and these accumulators race to completion. The first accumulator
to finish determines both the chosen response and the observed response time.

The LNR works with two or more response alternatives and has fewer parameters
than the Linear Ballistic Accumulator or the Diffusion Decision Model. This
makes it a good starting point for decomposing RT distributions, especially in
multi-alternative tasks.

## Model specification

Each response alternative $k$ has an accumulator whose finishing time $T_k$
follows a lognormal distribution:

$$
T_k \sim \text{Lognormal}(\mu_k, \sigma)
$$

where $\mu_k$ is the meanlog parameter (lower values produce faster finishing
times) and $\sigma$ is the sdlog parameter controlling variability, called `s`
in `bmm`. Meanlog and sdlog are the mean and the standard deviation of
$\log T_k$, so they live on the log scale of the finishing time, not on the
scale of seconds. The observed response and response time are:

$$
\text{Response} = \arg\min_k T_k, \quad RT = \min_k T_k + \tau
$$

where $\tau$ is the non-decision time for stimulus encoding and motor
execution. Since the lognormal distribution is positively skewed and defined
on the positive reals, it fits the shape of empirical RT distributions well.

# Parametrization in the `bmm` package

The `bmm` package provides two versions of the LNR.

## Simple version (`version = "simple"`)

The simple version uses two meanlog parameters: one for correct responses
and one shared across all error responses.

| Parameter | Description | Link function |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|
| `correct` | Meanlog for the correct accumulator | identity |
| `error`   | Meanlog for all error accumulators | identity |
| `ndt`     | Non-decision time | log |
| `s`       | Sdlog, shared across accumulators | log |

Responses must be integer-coded (factor or character digits are converted): 1 for correct, 2 through K for errors. The
total number of alternatives is specified via `n_choices`. Use this
version for standard accuracy-based designs where the distinction between
correct and error processing is the primary interest.

## Custom version (`version = "custom"`)

The custom version assigns a separate meanlog parameter to each response
category. Category names are defined in the formula and matched to character
labels in the response column of the data:

| Parameter | Description | Link function |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|
| one per category | Meanlog for that category's accumulator(s) | identity |
| `ndt`     | Non-decision time | log |
| `s`       | Sdlog, shared across accumulators | log |

The custom version also supports per-category `accumulators` for tasks
where categories contain different numbers of items (e.g., 1 target, 3
similar lures, 5 unrelated distractors). A category with $n$ accumulators
has $n$ independent lognormal finishing times that share the category's
meanlog, and the category wins whenever the fastest of them is the fastest
overall. More accumulators in a category therefore make that category win
more often and faster, at the same meanlog. Category names must not use
reserved internal parameter names such as `mu`, `ndt`, or `s`, must not be
Stan reserved words, must not contain an underscore, and must not end in
numbers. Breaking these rules is an error, not a warning. When supplied
directly, `accumulators` must contain positive integers. When supplied via
columns, the counts must be non-negative integers: a column may hold 0 on
trials the category does not win, but it must hold at least 1 on every trial
the category wins.

Choose the custom version when the errors are of different kinds, for example
when one alternative is similar to the correct response and another is
unrelated to it, so that a single shared `error` meanlog would be too coarse.
The custom version still estimates a single `s`: all accumulators of all
categories share it.

## Identifiability

All four parameters are estimated by default, `s` among them. `s` is not a
scale constraint. That argument belongs to models whose accumulation is
measured in arbitrary evidence units — in the Linear Ballistic Accumulator,
multiplying the drift rates and the threshold by the same factor leaves the
likelihood unchanged, so one of them has to be pinned. Nothing of the sort
holds here: the finishing times of the LNR *are* the response times, observed
in seconds, and changing `s` changes both the shape of the predicted RT
distribution and the predicted accuracy.

The data are in fact quite informative about `s`. The table below profiles the
negative log-likelihood of 4000 simulated trials over a grid of `s`,
maximising the two meanlogs and the non-decision time at every grid point:

```{r}
set.seed(7)
prof_dat <- rlnr(n = 4000, m = c(-1, -0.5), s = 0.5, ndt = 0.3)
min_rt <- min(prof_dat$rt)

nll <- function(par, s, dat) {
  ndt <- min_rt * stats::plogis(par[3])
  -sum(dlnr(dat$rt, dat$response, m = par[1:2], s = s, ndt = ndt, log = TRUE))
}

profile_s <- as.data.frame(t(vapply(
  c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.5),
  function(s) {
    opt <- stats::optim(c(-1, -0.5, 0), nll, s = s, dat = prof_dat)
    c(s = s, nll = opt$value, correct = opt$par[1], error = opt$par[2],
      ndt = min_rt * stats::plogis(opt$par[3]))
  },
  numeric(5)
)))

free <- stats::optim(c(-1, -0.5, 0, log(0.5)),
                     function(par) nll(par[1:3], exp(par[4]), prof_dat))

round(profile_s, 3)
```

The profile bottoms out at the generating value of `r profile_s$s[which.min(profile_s$nll)]`,
and the freely estimated `s` lands at `r round(exp(free$par[4]), 3)`. Holding
`s` at 1 instead is worse by
`r round(profile_s$nll[profile_s$s == 1] - free$value)` log-likelihood units —
this is not a flat direction in the likelihood.

The other parameters do not stay put while `s` is held at the wrong value.
Reading down the table, the non-decision time climbs with `s` until it is
pressed against the fastest observed response time
(`r round(min_rt, 3)` s here, against a generating value of 0.3), and both
meanlogs move with it. That is what makes a wrong `s` expensive: it is paid
for by the parameters one usually wants to interpret.

You can still fix `s`, for instance to reproduce a published fit that held the
sdlog at 1. Write `s = 0` in the formula:
`bmf(correct ~ 1, error ~ 1, ndt ~ 1, s = 0)`. The function `bmf()` collects
the formulas of the model parameters and is introduced below. Constants in `bmf()` are read on
the parameter's own link scale, and `s` uses a log link, so `s = 0` means
sdlog = 1.

# Data requirements

## Simple version

The data must contain:

- An RT column with response times in **seconds**
- A response column with integer values: 1 = correct, 2:K = errors

```{r}
set.seed(42)
m_true <- c(-1, 0)
s_true <- 0.5
ndt_true <- 0.2

dat_simple <- rlnr(n = 2000, m = m_true, s = s_true, ndt = ndt_true)
str(dat_simple)
```

For a four-choice task, simulate four accumulators. The simple version pools
responses 2 through 4 into the single `error` parameter, so they share a
meanlog here as well:

```{r}
set.seed(43)
dat_k4 <- rlnr(n = 2000, m = c(-1, -0.2, -0.2, -0.2), s = 0.5, ndt = 0.2)
table(dat_k4$response)
```

## Custom version

The data must contain:

- An RT column with response times in **seconds**
- A response column with **character labels** matching the formula parameters

```{r}
set.seed(44)
sim <- rlnr(n = 2000, m = c(-1, -0.5, -0.2), s = 0.5, ndt = 0.15)
dat_custom <- data.frame(
  rt = sim$rt,
  resp = c("recall", "similar", "other")[sim$response]
)
str(dat_custom)
table(dat_custom$resp)
```

## Data preparation

The likelihood is zero for any response time at or below `ndt`, so the fastest
observed response time is an upper bound for `ndt`. A few implausibly fast
responses (anticipations, or key presses before the stimulus was processed)
therefore pull `ndt` towards zero and distort the other parameters. Trim such
trials before fitting, with a cutoff that is justified by the task.

# Fitting the model

Fitting takes three steps. A model object such as `lnr()` states the
response time and response columns and the version of the model. `bmf()`
collects one formula per model parameter. `bmm()` combines the formula, the
data and the model object, translates them into a `brms` model and runs the
sampler, so most arguments of `brms::brm()` (such as `iter`, `cores`,
`control` and `file`) can be passed on.

## Simple version: two-choice task

```{r, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
model <- lnr(rt = "rt", response = "response", n_choices = 2)

formula <- bmf(
  correct ~ 1,
  error ~ 1,
  ndt ~ 1,
  s ~ 1
)

fit <- bmm(formula, dat_simple, model,
           cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr",
           # Reduce iterations to keep file size manageable
           iter = 1000,
           warmup = 500,
           file = "assets/bmmfit_lnr_simple_vignette.rds")
```

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

`ndt` and `s` use a log link, so they have to be exponentiated before they are
compared with the values the data were simulated from:

```{r}
fixef_est <- brms::fixef(fit)

data.frame(
  parameter = c("correct", "error", "ndt", "s"),
  true = c(m_true, ndt_true, s_true),
  estimate = c(
    fixef_est["correct_Intercept", "Estimate"],
    fixef_est["error_Intercept", "Estimate"],
    exp(fixef_est["ndt_Intercept", "Estimate"]),
    exp(fixef_est["s_Intercept", "Estimate"])
  ),
  lower = c(
    fixef_est["correct_Intercept", "Q2.5"],
    fixef_est["error_Intercept", "Q2.5"],
    exp(fixef_est["ndt_Intercept", "Q2.5"]),
    exp(fixef_est["s_Intercept", "Q2.5"])
  ),
  upper = c(
    fixef_est["correct_Intercept", "Q97.5"],
    fixef_est["error_Intercept", "Q97.5"],
    exp(fixef_est["ndt_Intercept", "Q97.5"]),
    exp(fixef_est["s_Intercept", "Q97.5"])
  )
)
```

## Posterior predictive checks

A race model predicts two things at once, and a model can reproduce the
response time distribution while getting the choice proportions wrong, so both
are worth checking. `pp_check_vars()` lists the observables the LNR declares:

```{r}
pp_check_vars(fit)
```

The default check plots the response times. Passing `resp_var = "response"`
checks the winning category instead, as a bar plot of observed against
predicted response counts. The observable is called `"response"` in both
versions of the model, whatever the name of the response column in the data:

```{r, message=FALSE}
pp_check(fit)
```

```{r, message=FALSE}
pp_check(fit, resp_var = "response", type = "bars")
```

## Four-choice task

For a four-choice task, set `n_choices = 4`. Responses 2 through 4 all
share the `error` parameter:

```{r, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
model_k4 <- lnr(rt = "rt", response = "response", n_choices = 4)

fit_k4 <- bmm(bmf(correct ~ 1, error ~ 1, ndt ~ 1, s ~ 1),
              dat_k4, model_k4,
              cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr",
              iter = 1000,
              warmup = 500,
              file = "assets/bmmfit_lnr_k4_vignette.rds")
```

```{r}
summary(fit_k4)
```

## Custom version: named categories

```{r, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
model_custom <- lnr(rt = "rt", response = "resp", version = "custom")

formula_custom <- bmf(
  recall ~ 1,
  similar ~ 1,
  other ~ 1,
  ndt ~ 1,
  s ~ 1
)

fit_custom <- bmm(formula_custom, dat_custom, model_custom,
                  cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr",
                  iter = 1000,
                  warmup = 500,
                  file = "assets/bmmfit_lnr_custom_vignette.rds")
```

```{r}
summary(fit_custom)
```

## Per-category accumulator counts

When categories have different numbers of racing accumulators, pass a named
integer vector to `accumulators`:

```{r}
model_numalt <- lnr(
  rt = "rt", response = "resp", version = "custom",
  accumulators = c(recall = 1, similar = 3, other = 5)
)
```

If the number of items per category varies across trials, pass column names
instead of integers (e.g.,
`c(recall = "n_recall", similar = "n_similar", other = "n_other")`).

## Hierarchical models

Both versions can be specified with random effects. Hierarchical fits are the
more demanding case, because there are more parameters and fewer trials
informing each of them. Start with a simple random-effects structure and
slightly stricter sampler settings such as `adapt_delta = 0.95`, and treat
convergence diagnostics as a hard requirement before interpreting the
estimates.

```{r}
set.seed(45)
n_id <- 20
n_trials <- 60

dat_hier <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_id), function(id) {
  u_correct <- stats::rnorm(1, 0, 0.25)
  u_error <- stats::rnorm(1, 0, 0.25)
  u_ndt <- stats::rnorm(1, 0, 0.15)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("easy", "hard"), function(condition) {
    sim <- rlnr(
      n = n_trials,
      m = c(-1 + u_correct + 0.4 * (condition == "hard"), u_error),
      s = 0.5,
      ndt = 0.2 * exp(u_ndt)
    )
    data.frame(id = id, condition = condition,
               rt = sim$rt, response = sim$response)
  }))
}))
dat_hier$condition <- factor(dat_hier$condition, levels = c("easy", "hard"))
str(dat_hier)
```

```{r, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
model_hier <- lnr(rt = "rt", response = "response", n_choices = 2)

formula_hier <- bmf(
  correct ~ 1 + condition + (1 + condition | id),
  error ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  ndt ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  s ~ 1
)

fit_hier <- bmm(formula_hier, dat_hier, model_hier,
                cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr",
                iter = 1000,
                warmup = 500,
                control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
                file = "assets/bmmfit_lnr_hierarchical_vignette.rds")
```

```{r}
summary(fit_hier)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
np_hier <- brms::nuts_params(fit_hier)
n_div <- sum(np_hier$Value[np_hier$Parameter == "divergent__"])
max_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_hier), na.rm = TRUE)
```

This fit has `r n_div` divergent transitions and a maximum Rhat of
`r round(max_rhat, 3)`. Group-level standard deviations of parameters with a
log link (`ndt` here) are on the log scale, like the intercepts, while the
standard deviations of the meanlog parameters are on the meanlog scale.

As criteria for a usable fit, we look for a maximum Rhat below 1.01, no
divergent transitions, and bulk effective sample sizes in the hundreds. The
maximum Rhat in this article is always `max(brms::rhat(fit), na.rm = TRUE)`,
the largest value over all parameters of the fit, including the group-level
effects and `lp__` (the constant `mu` gives `NA`, hence `na.rm`). The
divergent transitions are counted by
`sum(brms::nuts_params(fit)$Parameter == "divergent__" & brms::nuts_params(fit)$Value == 1)`.
The bulk ESS is in the `Bulk_ESS` column of `summary(fit)`; its smallest
population-level value for `fit_hier` is
`r round(min(summary(fit_hier)$fixed$Bulk_ESS, na.rm = TRUE))`. The table
printed by `summary()` shows the population-level rows only, so its largest
Rhat (`r round(max(summary(fit_hier)$fixed$Rhat, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`) is
smaller than the maximum over all parameters.

## Hierarchical custom version

The custom version takes random effects in the same way. The example has three
response categories and 15 simulated participants with 80 trials each. Every
participant has their own intercept for each category and for `ndt`; the
generating values are meanlogs of -1, -0.5 and -0.2, `ndt` of 0.2 s (log scale
-1.61), and `s` of 0.5 (log scale -0.69).

```{r}
set.seed(46)
n_id_ch <- 15
n_trials_ch <- 80
m_cat <- c(recall = -1, similar = -0.5, other = -0.2)

dat_ch <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_id_ch), function(id) {
  u <- stats::rnorm(4, 0, c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.15))
  sim <- rlnr(n = n_trials_ch, m = m_cat + u[1:3], s = 0.5,
              ndt = 0.2 * exp(u[4]))
  data.frame(id = id, rt = sim$rt, resp = names(m_cat)[sim$response])
}))
str(dat_ch)
```

```{r, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
formula_ch <- bmf(
  recall ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  similar ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  other ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  ndt ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  s ~ 1
)

fit_ch <- bmm(formula_ch, dat_ch, model_custom,
              cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr",
              iter = 1000,
              warmup = 500,
              thin = 4,
              control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
              file = "assets/bmmfit_lnr_custom_hierarchical_vignette.rds")
```

The cached fit is thinned (`thin = 4`) to keep the file small.

```{r}
summary(fit_ch)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
np_ch <- brms::nuts_params(fit_ch)
n_div_ch <- sum(np_ch$Value[np_ch$Parameter == "divergent__"])
hyp_ch <- brms::hypothesis(fit_ch, "recall_Intercept - similar_Intercept < 0")$hypothesis
max_rhat_ch <- max(brms::rhat(fit_ch), na.rm = TRUE)
```

The fit has `r n_div_ch` divergent transitions and a maximum Rhat of
`r round(max_rhat_ch, 3)`, computed as described above. That is slightly above
the criterion of 1.01 (the largest population-level value is the Rhat of
`s_Intercept`, `r round(summary(fit_ch)$fixed["s_Intercept", "Rhat"], 3)`). This
example is shortened and thinned to keep the cached file small. A real analysis
would run more iterations and check that Rhat falls below 1.01 before
interpreting the estimates. The intercepts are close to the generating values
once `ndt` and `s` are put back on the natural scale: `exp(ndt_Intercept)` is
`r round(exp(brms::fixef(fit_ch)["ndt_Intercept", "Estimate"]), 2)` s against
0.2, and `exp(s_Intercept)` is
`r round(exp(brms::fixef(fit_ch)["s_Intercept", "Estimate"]), 2)` against 0.5.

```{r, message=FALSE}
pp_check(fit_ch, resp_var = "response", type = "bars")
```

A contrast between two category intercepts is a linear hypothesis on the
population-level coefficients. Here we test whether the `recall` accumulator
is faster than the `similar` accumulator, which means a smaller meanlog:

```{r}
brms::hypothesis(fit_ch, "recall_Intercept - similar_Intercept < 0")
```

The posterior mean of the difference is `r round(hyp_ch$Estimate, 2)` (90%
interval from `r round(hyp_ch$CI.Lower, 2)` to `r round(hyp_ch$CI.Upper, 2)`),
the evidence ratio is `r if (is.infinite(hyp_ch$Evid.Ratio)) "infinite" else round(hyp_ch$Evid.Ratio, 1)` and the posterior probability is
`r hyp_ch$Post.Prob`: none of the retained draws has `recall` slower than
`similar`. The generating difference is -0.5 and lies inside the interval. The
meanlogs are locations of the log finishing time of a latent accumulator, so
`exp(difference)`, here `r round(exp(hyp_ch$Estimate), 2)`, is a ratio of the median finishing times of the two accumulators. It is not a
ratio of observed response times, because the observed response time is the
minimum over the race.

# Default priors

| Parameter | Prior | Scale |
|-----------|-------|-------|
| `correct` | `normal(-1, 0.5)` | identity (meanlog) |
| `error` | `normal(0, 0.5)` | identity (meanlog) |
| `ndt` | `normal(-1.5, 0.5)` | log (median 0.22s on the natural scale) |
| `s` | `normal(0, 0.5)` | log (median 1, 95% between 0.37 and 2.7) |

For the custom version, category parameters default to `normal(0, 0.5)` on
the identity scale. The `ndt` prior is the one the **ddm** model uses:
multi-alternative choice tasks carry longer non-decision times than the
two-boundary models in `bmm` were first calibrated on, and a prior whose upper
range sits below the true value biases the meanlogs with it. The prior on
`s` puts its median at a sdlog of 1 while leaving room for the values RT data
are usually fitted at.

Check the priors of a given model and formula with `default_prior()` and
adjust them as needed:

```{r}
default_prior(formula, dat_simple, model)
```

The unnamed `constant(0)` row is the internal parameter `mu`, a placeholder
that the model needs for the `brms` family and that is fixed at 0. It does
not enter the likelihood and should be left at its default.

The default `normal(0, 0.5)` for the categories of the custom version is
centered at a meanlog of 0, a median finishing time of one second. The
default recovers the `recall` category of the examples above (true meanlog of
-1) well, but if you know a category is much faster or slower than that, a
prior centered there is the first thing to adjust. Priors are passed to `bmm()` through
`prior`, with the category named in `dpar`. The table below shows the default
priors of two categories, before any change:

```{r}
default_prior(formula_custom, dat_custom, model_custom) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  subset(dpar %in% c("recall", "similar"), select = c(prior, class, dpar))
```

The following call replaces the default of `recall` by `normal(-1, 0.5)`. It is
not run here, to avoid a refit.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
prior_custom <- brms::prior(normal(-1, 0.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "recall")

fit_custom_prior <- bmm(formula_custom, dat_custom, model_custom,
                        prior = prior_custom,
                        cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr",
                        iter = 1000,
                        warmup = 500)
```

`stancode()` shows that the prior was picked up, without running the sampler:

```{r}
prior_custom <- brms::prior(normal(-1, 0.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "recall")
stancode(formula_custom, dat_custom, model_custom, prior = prior_custom) |>
  strsplit("\n") |>
  unlist() |>
  grep(pattern = "lprior \\+= normal_lpdf\\(Intercept_recall", value = TRUE)
```

# References
